draft.title: The digestive system
card: Digestion breaks large food molecules into small ones that can pass into the blood. Food is broken down in two ways: physically, into smaller pieces, and chemically, by enzymes.
Mouth and stomach
Teeth chew food into small pieces, and saliva begins to break down starch. In the stomach, muscles churn the food and acid and enzymes break down protein.
Small intestine
Most chemical digestion ends here. Its wall is folded into tiny villi, which give a large surface area. The small molecules are absorbed through the villi into the blood.
Large intestine
It takes in water from the leftover material. The remains leave the body as faeces.
draft.remember: Digestion makes food molecules small enough to absorb, and the small intestine passes them into the blood.

a.q: Where do digested food molecules pass into the blood?
opts: The small intestine
The stomach
The large intestine
The mouth
a.why: The small intestine has villi that give a large surface area, and the small molecules pass through them into the blood. The stomach is tempting because it digests food, but the card says the stomach breaks food down and does not absorb it.
a.clue: Look for the part with villi.

b.q: Sam swallows a mouthful of food without chewing it. Which change would make digestion slower?
opts: Larger pieces give enzymes less surface to work on
Saliva would turn the food into large molecules
The villi would not be able to absorb water
Acid in the stomach would stop breaking down protein
b.why: Chewing breaks food into small pieces, which gives enzymes more surface to work on. Without it, larger pieces are digested more slowly. Stomach acid still works on protein, so that option is wrong.
b.clue: Think about what chewing does to the size of the pieces.

b.best: Larger pieces give enzymes less surface to work on

problems.detail: The card never says that smaller pieces give enzymes more surface to work on. It mentions surface area only for the villi, so the question needs more than the card teaches.

card: Digestion breaks large food molecules into small ones that can pass into the blood. Enzymes are chemicals made by the body that break these molecules apart.

a.q: Where do digested food molecules pass into the blood?
opts: The small intestine
The stomach
The large intestine
The mouth
a.why: The small intestine absorbs the small molecules through its villi into the blood. The stomach is tempting because a lot of digestion happens there, but breaking food down is not the same as absorbing it, and the card gives absorption to the small intestine.
a.clue: Absorbing means taking in, not breaking down.

b.q: Sam swallows a mouthful of food without chewing it. Why would this food be digested more slowly?
opts: Large pieces give enzymes less surface to work on
Large pieces pass straight into the large intestine
Enzymes work only after food reaches the large intestine
Chewing is the only step that breaks down protein
b.why: Chewing breaks food into small pieces, which gives enzymes more surface to work on. Without it, enzymes reach less of the food at once, so digestion is slower. Protein is broken down in the stomach by acid and enzymes, not by chewing, so that option is wrong.
b.clue: Think about how much of the food the enzymes can reach.
